source.title: Recurrence Is Not Enough: Causally Validating Multilingual SAE Translation Features in Gemma 2 and 3
source.authors: Giang Nguyen; Nhi Thi Yen Nguyen; W. Buntine; Dung D. Le

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study causally tests whether recurring SAE features transfer across language settings. Its results refine the claim that recurrence evidences a transferable mechanism: most recurring candidates lack a consistent causal effect, while one feature per model transfers robustly.
record.gate_note: The paper directly discovers and intervenes on SAE translation-initiation features, reporting COMET outcomes. Rows below cover the transferable feature's reported Gemma 2 results across all 23 settings, Gemma 3 results in the four discovery settings and its stated no-effect exception, plus the paper's aggregate account of the other 21 recurring features. The paper also reports chrF++, non-translation fractions, dose-response, and task-specificity checks; those additional metrics are not separately extracted here. Discovery counts and PCA thresholds are not intervention outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs as a tool and asks whether recurring translation-initiation features keep a causal role across prompt, source and target languages. Its measure, COMET change under feature amplification or ablation, is a causal-transfer score for chosen features. It does not test superposition in toy models (V1) or the capacity account (V2). It does not test non-capacity polysemanticity (V3). It does not measure whether features are spread across neurons or how well an SAE recovers sparse features (V4). It does not test SAE completeness, stability across SAE runs, or canonicality (V5), or feature dimensionality (V6). The finding that recurrence fails to predict causal effect concerns how reliable feature selection is, a related but different construct. It is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Recurrence is a weak proxy for causal transfer: 22 features recur per model, but only one per model improves COMET when amplified and degrades it when ablated across most of 23 settings. The authors read it as a language-agnostic translation-initiation direction. Results are limited to the two Gemma models with 16k Gemma Scope SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: Follows the three-stage discovery and intervention protocol of Wu et al. (2026), using their published codebase and thresholds, but varies prompt, source, and target languages; evaluates 23 settings and adds Gemma 3 4B IT. The intervention is at the last prompt token with α=0 or α=2, and COMET is the primary metric.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome differs across features and settings: most recurring candidates are weak or inconsistent; the Gemma 3 feature has no significant effect in ar2en_ar. The paper also reports a dose-response pattern for the selected feature: α=0 hurts, moderate amplification helps, and larger coefficients may saturate or reverse.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma 2 2B IT and Gemma 3 4B IT, 22 SAE features recur across four discovery settings and pass PCA consistency. Only one per model, (L10, 5717) and (L20, 2456), shows consistent positive-amplification and negative-ablation COMET effects. That feature transfers across 23 language settings in Gemma 2 and 22 of 23 in Gemma 3. The other 21 per model are small, inconsistent or opposite in sign (Tables 3–5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recurrence of an SAE feature across contexts is a weak proxy for that feature having a consistent causal role; causal validation selects far fewer features than activation-based discovery.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 9th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP
record.problems: Evidence is limited to Gemma 2 2B IT and Gemma 3 4B IT with their corresponding SAEs. Discovery uses 98 examples and intervention uses the remainder of 960 examples. Discovery languages/settings are limited, and the authors say prompt language and translation direction cannot be fully disentangled. Results rely primarily on COMET; the authors note it may not capture adequacy or fluency fully. Features are evaluated individually, not in combined interventions. The aggregate rows for the 21 other recurring features omit their displayed per-feature table values.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports individual Table 3 and Table 4 outcomes for 21 non-selected recurring features per model, and Tables 6–11 report non-translation fractions, task-specificity, chrF++, and further transfer-setting outcomes. Due to the 60-row limit, only the authors' aggregate account of the 21-feature groups, the full Gemma 2 selected-feature COMET results, the four Gemma 3 discovery settings, and Gemma 3's reported no-effect exception are retained. Other Gemma 3 transfer-setting entries and ancillary metrics are not extracted.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no capacity or importance analysis of neurons.
SAEs are used off the shelf. There is no measure of feature distribution across neurons, SAE reconstruction, or sparse-feature recovery quality.

Completeness, stability across SAE training runs or widths, and canonicality are not tested. A small-L0 SAE preliminary yielded only 4 PCA-consistent features, but this is anecdotal and not analysed as an SAE-stability result.
All: no comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V4 and V5 and gave supports/limits_scope labels. I reject these links. The paper never measures superposition or SAE recovery quality, and cross-lingual causal transfer of a chosen feature is not SAE-feature canonicality or completeness. Toy Models of Superposition is only cited. Uncertainty for R01–R50 is the paired bootstrap with one-sided p<0.05, except values marked †.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Polysemanticity as competition for limited capacity and importance-dependent dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Polysemanticity from causes other than superposition.

The paper tests whether specific SAE-recovered translation features have causal effects across settings; it does not measure how broadly features are distributed across neurons or recover general-purpose feature dictionaries.

Cross-setting causal consistency is tested for translation-initiation features; completeness and canonicality of SAE features, and their stability beyond the tested models, tasks, and settings, are not established.
The paper intervenes on SAE feature activations but does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features or test superposition geometry.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma 2 2B IT and Gemma 3 4B IT; tested translation settings for each model
reader_labels.reason: The recovered SAE feature in each model has causal translation-quality effects under intervention: amplification improves and ablation generally degrades COMET (Gemma 2 rows R01–R42; Gemma 3 rows R43–R50). This supports the specific tested case of an SAE-recoverable feature, not broad claims about feature distributions.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The selected feature in each tested model across the reported discovery settings
reader_labels.reason: The selected SAE feature has repeatable causal effects across the four discovery settings, although Gemma 3 amplification in zh2ja_en is modest (R01–R08, R43–R50).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The other recurring candidates in the four discovery settings; also Gemma 3 ar2en_ar
reader_labels.reason: Most recurring features do not show the expected consistent causal signature, and the Gemma 3 selected feature has no significant effect in ar2en_ar. Recurrence therefore does not establish cross-setting causal stability for every candidate (R51–R56).
